name: Press Taylor

views.text: Play to win instead of playing not to lose; aggressive football is a choice you make every week.
If the quarterback does not believe in a call, it does not belong on the sheet.
Online criticism is noise; results end the argument.
Change is how a coach grows; stepping back from calling plays to learn another system is part of that.
The best trick plays are drawn up by assistants who live in the building.
Winning is the only thing that matters; everything else, including who calls plays, serves that.
A coordinator who does not call plays earns his keep at halftime and in the meeting room.

signatures: mentions the hours and the reading he puts into the job when asked about pressure
credits the quarterback's input on the call sheet when a game plan works
defers to the head coach on anything about play-calling

motivation.want: to prove he is a play-caller in his own right, not a protege
motivation.fear: that past struggles that cost his mentor a job define him

want.text: to help build a winner in Chicago

voice: Intense and earnest, with a younger coach's conviction; he speaks about aggression, growth and winning, brushes off criticism without heat, and spreads credit across the staff and the quarterback. In Chicago he says little in public and defers to the head coach on play-calling, so his recent public record is thin.

evidence.summary: Office visit with Taylor: football and leadership books, roughly 100-hour weeks in season, helped draw up the Philly Special as Eagles assistant quarterbacks coach, wants a team that plays to win rather than avoids mistakes, shrugs off online criticism; describes a collaborative call sheet where Pederson and assistants weigh in and Lawrence ranks plays he believes in. Independent newsletter; his self-description.

Pederson keeps Taylor as play-caller after the offense regressed in 2023, saying it can be better and blaming mainly execution, including Lawrence's 21 turnovers; Taylor has been on every Pederson staff since 2016, and Pederson reportedly wanted to promote him to coordinator in Philadelphia. Opinion framing; the writer thinks it is risky.

After a 24-20 loss at Houston dropped the team to 0-4, Pederson refuses to take play-calling back from Taylor, says Taylor called a strong game and that coaches cannot make the plays, then redirects criticism to himself. Firm and protective of his staff.

After a late 2023 fade, first-time play-caller Taylor took much of the blame; he says winning comes first and frames possible changes around helping the team improve, pointing to Lawrence and offseason physical growth; Pederson says the roster needed fixing; no decision yet on who calls plays.

evidence.publisher: Associated Press via News4JAX, Mark Long
evidence.summary: Jacksonville fires Pederson after 4-13, its 18th loss in 23 games; owner Shad Khan cites predictability on both sides of the ball and a 3-10 record in one-score games; Pederson made the playoffs in year one but did not develop Lawrence or build an identity, and kept Taylor calling plays against Khan's wishes; Christian Kirk says Pederson made him a better player and man.

Chicago promotes him from pass-game coordinator, his 2025 role on Ben Johnson's first staff, to offensive coordinator, replacing Declan Doyle, who left to call plays in Baltimore. Johnson keeps calling plays. Notes his 2022-24 Jacksonville coordinator stint. Facts only; no quotes.

He takes over Doyle's duties: leading offensive meetings when Johnson cannot and handling halftime adjustments. Johnson says Taylor is natural in front of the room, respected by the staff and knows how to steer the meeting when Johnson is away. Taylor himself is not quoted.
